Stands with similar soils, management histories, or forest types may differ
in tree density and species composition even after accounting for canopy
height. We represent such groups as strata and extend the
[full plot-sampling model](full-model-plot-sampling.html) with a magnitude
random intercept and a species factor effect for each stratum.

We use three groups of stands to generate a new population. We then fit
the model, check the chains, and compare combined intercepts by stratum with
their generating values in a table and maps. Finally, we
predict across the forest and compare forest, stratum, and stand
species-by-DBH densities with truth.
The canopy-height slopes and the DBH allocation models remain the same
across strata.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}

Extract it and use the folder containing `data/` as your R working directory.
We generate the stratum effects and tree counts below.
:::

## Read the prepared data

We created three strata of 83 stands each for this example, using the
stand boundaries and canopy heights from the shared inventory data. We read the
prepared locations, which already have `stratum_id`, sampled areas, and
canopy-height predictors, along with the forest, stands, and plot locations
for mapping.

```{r}
#| label: read-spatial-data
```

The `dataset` column identifies observed plot units and prediction units.
Units crossing stratum boundaries have been divided into portions, each
with its own `plot_id`, area, and stratum. We simulate counts separately for
each portion. Applying this construction to field data would require counts
recorded by portion. The predictor `x` uses the same
standardization as in the [data article](plot-sampling-data.html).

We map the strata and the 151 sampled plot locations.

```{r}

#| fig-height: 7

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = stands, aes(fill = factor(stratum_id)), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = forest, fill = NA, color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = plot_centers, shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 1.5,
          stroke = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#009E73", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9"),
                    name = "Stratum") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

## Generate a population with stratum effects

### Magnitude and species models

For observed unit $i$, let $a_i$ be its area in hectares, $x_i$ its
standardized canopy height, and $g(i)$ its stratum. The magnitude model is

$$
\log M_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\delta_{g(i)},\qquad
\delta_g\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma_\delta^2),\qquad
N_i\mid M_i,r_M\sim\operatorname{NB}(a_iM_i,r_M).
$$

Here $M_i$ is expected tree density in trees/ha, $N_i$ is total count, and
$r_M$ is negative-binomial size. The combined intercept
$\beta_0+\delta_g$ gives log expected density in stratum $g$ at average
plot canopy height. The stratum effect multiplies expected density by
$\exp(\delta_g)$ at a given canopy height; the canopy-height slope $\beta_1$
is shared across strata.

Species allocation proceeds through pine, then oak, with birch receiving
the remaining trees. For allocation step $j$, its conditional probability is

$$
\pi_{ij}=\Phi(\alpha_{0j}+\alpha_{1j}x_i+\gamma_j u_{g(i)}),
\qquad u_g\sim\operatorname{N}(0,1),
$$

where $\Phi$ is the standard Normal distribution function, implemented by
`pnorm()`. Each stratum has one factor score $u_g$, shared by the two
allocation steps. The loadings $\gamma_j$ determine how that score changes
each step. Pine is the anchor, so its loading is positive; oak's loading
can have either sign. Fixing the factor variance at one allows the
loadings to determine the amount of variation among strata.

For this population, we use $\beta_0=\log(350)$, $\beta_1=-0.2$,
$\sigma_\delta=0.5$, and $r_M=1000$. The simpler examples used $r_M=50$
and estimated it during fitting. Here we fix size at its generating value
because magComp does not estimate it alongside magnitude random effects.
The species intercepts and slopes match the earlier articles. Loadings of
0.7 for pine and $-0.5$ for oak
make a larger factor score favor pine allocation and reduce oak allocation
among the remaining trees. Birch has no separate allocation coefficient.

We draw each stratum's magnitude effect and species score once, then use
them for all its observed and prediction units. The magnitude effects and
species scores are independent in this model. Their generating distributions
have mean zero, but the three realized effects need not average to zero.

## Fit the stratum model

We arrange the observed counts into one row per unit, species, and DBH
class. The category ordering matches the allocation sequence used above.

```{r}
#| label: model-data

library(magComp)

species_order <- c("pine", "oak", "birch")

trees <- plots |>
  select(plot_id, stratum_id, area, x, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)
  ) |>
  arrange(plot_id, species, dbh_class)

dat <- magCompData(
  trees,
  unit = plot_id, categories = c(species, dbh_class),
  tree_count = count, design = fixedArea(area)
)
```

`iid()` adds the magnitude random intercept. `factor_iid()` adds the
shared species factor, with `K = 1` specifying one score per stratum.
The term names identify their samples in the fitted object.

```{r}
#| label: fit

fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = ~ x + iid(stratum_id, name = "stratum_intercept"),
  composition = magCompComposition(
    species ~ x + factor_iid(stratum_id, K = 1, anchors = "pine",
                             name = "stratum_intercept"),
    dbh_class | species ~ x
  ),
  control = magCompControl(
    n_samples = 4000,
    n_burn = 1000,
    n_chains = 3,
    n_cores = 3,
    chain_seeds = 1:3,
    nb_size = 1000,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)
```

We retain automatic starting values and default priors. The magnitude
random-effect variance and species loadings are estimated. Each of three
chains contributes 3,000 retained draws after discarding 1,000 burn-in iterations.

The group effects share a distribution, which lets information from other
strata help estimate each effect. This is often called partial pooling.
Here only three strata inform the between-stratum variation, even though
there are many observed units within them.

## Check the chains

We begin with `summary(fit)` and add the generating values for comparison.
The table focuses on the magnitude and species parameters; the complete
summary also includes the DBH coefficients. R-hat values near one indicate
agreement among chains. ESS is the effective sample size after accounting
for dependence among draws.

```{r}
#| label: separate-parameters

parameter_summary <- summary(fit)

true_parameters <- tribble(
  ~component,    ~parameter,      ~index,              ~truth,
  "magnitude",   "coefficients",  "(Intercept)",       beta_0,
  "magnitude",   "coefficients",  "x",                 beta_1,
  "magnitude",   "variance",      "",                  sigma_delta^2,
  "composition", "coefficients",  "pine:(Intercept)",  alpha_pine[1],
  "composition", "coefficients",  "pine:x",            alpha_pine[2],
  "composition", "coefficients",  "oak:(Intercept)",   alpha_oak[1],
  "composition", "coefficients",  "oak:x",             alpha_oak[2],
  "composition", "loadings",      "pine:pine",         gamma_pine,
  "composition", "loadings",      "oak:pine",          gamma_oak
)

main_parameters <- parameter_summary |>
  filter(component == "magnitude" | block == "species") |>
  left_join(true_parameters, by = c("component", "parameter", "index"))

main_parameters |>
  select(symbol, truth, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Parameter", "Truth", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R-hat", "ESS"))
```

The canopy-height slopes have R-hats near one. The magnitude intercept,
however, has an R-hat of 1.429 and a small ESS. The species intercepts and
loadings also mix slowly, as indicated by R-hats of 1.225 and 1.209 for
the pine and oak intercepts and 1.175 and 1.157 for their respective loadings.

An overall intercept and its random effects can trade off while leaving
fitted values nearly unchanged. For magnitude, an increase in $\beta_0$
can be offset by decreases in the $\delta_g$, keeping the combined
intercepts $\beta_0+\delta_g$ similar. The species models have an analogous
sum, $\alpha_{0j}+\gamma_j u_g$. The counts inform these sums more directly
than their separate components, especially with only three strata.

We use `samples(fit, type = "combined")` to add each regression coefficient
to its random effects within matching posterior draws and chains. For
species, this includes multiplying loadings by factor scores. Setting
`group = ".all"` averages these combined coefficients across fitted units,
so the diagnostic describes an average rather than an individual stratum.

```{r}
#| label: diagnostics

diagnostics <- samples(fit, type = "combined", group = ".all")

summary(diagnostics) |>
  transmute(quantity = if_else(component == "magnitude", "Magnitude",
                                paste(str_to_title(stick), "allocation")),
            rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Quantity", "R-hat", "ESS"))
```

The combined intercepts have R-hats close to one and much larger ESS.
In trace plots, this tradeoff can appear as separate intercept chains
moving slowly or staying at different levels, while the combined intercept
chains overlap and move through similar values. `plot(fit, parameters = "(Intercept)")`
shows the magnitude intercept chains, and `plot(diagnostics)` shows the combined chains.

The improved diagnostics apply specifically to the combined intercepts.

## Estimate and map combined intercepts by stratum

We now estimate each stratum's combined intercept and compare it with truth.

`summary()` uses the same sample extraction and combination as above.
With `group = "stratum_id"`, it averages within each stratum. Here each
stratum shares one combined intercept, so this returns its posterior mean,
95% credible interval, and chain diagnostics directly. The table includes
R-hat and ESS for each stratum's combined intercept.

```{r}
#| label: intercept-estimates

intercept_summary <- summary(fit, type = "combined", group = "stratum_id") |>
  mutate(component = if_else(component == "magnitude", "Magnitude",
                              str_to_title(stick))) |>
  rename(stratum_id = group) |>
  left_join(true_intercepts, by = c("component", "stratum_id"))

intercept_summary |>
  select(component, stratum_id, truth, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Component", "Stratum", "Truth", "Mean",
                             "2.5%", "97.5%", "R-hat", "ESS"))
```

Combined magnitude intercepts are on the log-density scale. Applying `exp()`
gives expected trees/ha at average plot canopy height. Combined species
intercepts are on the probit scale. Applying `pnorm()` gives pine's allocation
probability or oak's probability among the non-pine trees at that same canopy
height. To summarize densities or probabilities, apply these transformations
to each posterior draw before calculating means and intervals. The combined
intercept estimates closely match their generating values in this example.

We join the combined intercepts to stands through `stratum_id` and map truth
beside the posterior mean. Truth and estimates use the same color scale within
each figure. Stands in the same stratum share a combined intercept; their
densities and allocations still vary with canopy height.

```{r}
#| label: intercept-map-data

map_values <- intercept_summary |>
  select(stratum_id, component, Truth = truth, Estimate = mean) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Truth, Estimate), names_to = "source", values_to = "intercept") |>
  mutate(
    component = factor(component, levels = c("Magnitude", "Pine", "Oak")),
    source = factor(source, levels = c("Truth", "Estimate"))
  )

intercept_maps <- stands |>
  left_join(map_values, by = "stratum_id", relationship = "many-to-many")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-magnitude-intercepts
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "True and estimated combined magnitude intercepts by stratum, shown on the log-density scale."

ggplot(filter(intercept_maps, component == "Magnitude")) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = intercept), color = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~ source, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Combined\nintercept\n(log-density)") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-species-intercepts
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "True and estimated combined species allocation intercepts by stratum, shown on a common probit scale. Oak allocation is conditional on a tree not being pine."

ggplot(filter(intercept_maps, component %in% c("Pine", "Oak"))) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = intercept), color = NA) +
  facet_grid(component ~ source) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Combined\nintercept\n(probit)") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

The maps show differences among strata without a spatial random effect.
The model uses stratum membership, not distance between stands, to share
information. The table provides uncertainty that is not shown in the maps.

## Predict and summarize the forest

All prediction units belong to strata represented in the fit. Within each
posterior draw, `predict()` uses the sampled effect for that stratum,
generates a total count, and allocates it among species and DBH classes.
`type = "density"` divides these counts by each unit's area.

```{r}
#| label: predict

predictions <- predict(
  fit,
  prediction |> select(plot_id, stratum_id, x, area),
  type = "density",
  target = "observation",
  n_draws = 100,
  summary = "samples"
)

forest_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = prediction,
  unit = plot_id,
  represented_area = area,
  summary = "samples"
)

forest_summary <- summary(forest_predictions)
```

As in the full-model article, `standSummary()` averages densities using unit
areas within each draw. Stratum effects are already included in the predictions.
The 100 draws per chain give 300 forest draws, which we summarize and compare
with the simulated forest densities.

```{r}
#| label: forest-comparison

forest_truth <- prediction |>
  select(contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(species, dbh_class) |>
  summarise(truth = sum(count) / sum(prediction$area), .groups = "drop")

comparison <- forest_summary |>
  as_tibble() |>
  separate_wider_delim(category, delim = ":", names = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  left_join(forest_truth, by = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Forest species-by-DBH densities. Blue points and bars show posterior predictive means and 95% intervals; black horizontal marks show simulated truth."

ggplot(comparison, aes(dbh_class, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.15,
                color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth, shape = "Truth"), size = 6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Truth" = 95, "Estimate" = 16),
                     breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ species, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "DBH class (cm)", y = "Trees per hectare") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The estimates reproduce pine's relatively broad DBH distribution and the
greater concentration of oak and birch in the smaller classes.
These forest estimates combine the stratum-specific relationships with
canopy height and area across the prediction grid.

## Summarize predictions by stratum

Each prediction unit belongs to one stratum. Adding `group = stratum_id`
to the same `standSummary()` call gives species-by-DBH densities for each
stratum from the existing prediction draws.

```{r}
#| label: stratum-summary

stratum_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = prediction,
  unit = plot_id,
  group = stratum_id,
  represented_area = area,
  summary = "samples"
)
```

We calculate each stratum's true densities by dividing its simulated counts
by the summed area of its prediction units, then compare them with estimates
and intervals.

```{r}
#| label: stratum-comparison

stratum_truth <- prediction |>
  select(stratum_id, area, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(stratum_id, category) |>
  summarise(truth = sum(count) / sum(area), .groups = "drop")

stratum_comparison <- summary(stratum_predictions) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(stratum_id = as.integer(unit), stratum = paste("Stratum", stratum_id)) |>
  left_join(stratum_truth, by = c("stratum_id", "category"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-stratum-densities
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Estimated versus true species-by-DBH densities within each stratum. Each point represents one species-by-DBH category; bars show 95% posterior predictive intervals. Dashed lines mark equality."

density_limits <- c(0, max(stratum_comparison$truth, stratum_comparison$q97_5))

ggplot(stratum_comparison, aes(truth, mean)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0,
                color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ stratum, nrow = 1) +
  coord_equal(xlim = density_limits, ylim = density_limits) +
  labs(x = "True density (trees/ha)", y = "Estimated density (trees/ha)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Summarize predictions by stand

Some prediction units span several stands within a stratum. Following the
[data article](plot-sampling-data.html#cell-areas-within-stands), we calculate
their areas within stands using this example's prediction-unit polygons and IDs.

```{r}
#| label: stand-overlap-areas

prediction_units <- st_read(
  "data/stratum_prediction_units.gpkg", quiet = TRUE
)

# IDs remain labels when polygons are divided into overlapping parts.
st_agr(prediction_units) <- "constant"
st_agr(stands) <- "constant"

unit_stand_areas <- st_intersection(
  prediction_units |> select(plot_id),
  stands |> select(stand_id)
)

unit_stand_areas$area_ha <- as.numeric(st_area(unit_stand_areas)) / 10000

unit_stand_areas <- unit_stand_areas |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  filter(area_ha > 0) |>
  arrange(plot_id, stand_id)

# Prediction unit 72 overlaps two stands.
unit_stand_areas |>
  filter(plot_id == 72) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

We pass these overlap areas to `standSummary()` with `group = stand_id`.
Each unit's density draw is reused in every stand it overlaps, weighted by
the overlap area. This gives species-by-DBH densities and 95% posterior
predictive intervals for all 249 stands.

```{r}
#| label: stand-summary

stand_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = unit_stand_areas,
  unit = plot_id,
  group = stand_id,
  represented_area = area_ha,
  summary = "samples"
)

stand_summary <- summary(stand_predictions)
```

We calculate truth from the simulated category counts divided by unit area,
using the same overlap weights and constant density within each unit.

```{r}
#| label: stand-comparison

unit_truth <- prediction |>
  select(plot_id, area, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(density = count / area) |>
  select(plot_id, category, density)

stand_truth <- unit_stand_areas |>
  left_join(unit_truth, by = "plot_id", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  group_by(stand_id, category) |>
  summarise(truth = weighted.mean(density, area_ha), .groups = "drop")

stand_comparison <- stand_summary |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(stand_id = unit) |>
  left_join(stand_truth, by = c("stand_id", "category")) |>
  separate_wider_delim(category, delim = ":", names = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)
  )
```

We show all 15 species-by-DBH categories for one stand, with truth alongside
the estimates and intervals. Change `example_stand` to inspect another stand.

```{r}
#| label: example-stand

example_stand <- first(stand_comparison$stand_id)

stand_comparison |>
  filter(stand_id == example_stand) |>
  arrange(species, dbh_class) |>
  select(species, dbh_class, truth, mean, q2_5, q97_5) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
               col.names = c("Species", "DBH class", "Truth", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%"),
               caption = paste("Stand", example_stand))
```

The figure compares estimates with truth across all stands. Each species panel
contains five DBH-class estimates per stand, with faint interval bars to keep
overlapping estimates visible.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stand-densities
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Estimated versus true species-by-DBH densities for all 249 stands. Each panel contains 1,245 estimates (five DBH classes per stand); vertical bars show 95% posterior predictive intervals. Dashed lines mark equality. Axis ranges match within each panel and vary by species."

# Give both axes the same upper limit within each species panel.
stand_limits <- stand_comparison |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(limit = max(truth, mean, q97_5), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(stand_comparison, aes(truth, mean)) +
  geom_blank(data = stand_limits, aes(x = limit, y = limit)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0,
                color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 0.9, alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ species, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "True density (trees/ha)", y = "Estimated density (trees/ha)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

The [varying-slopes article](stratum-slopes-plot-sampling.html) extends this model
so canopy-height relationships can also differ among strata, in both magnitude
and species allocation.

The [spatial-effects article](spatial-effects-plot-sampling.html) represents processes
that vary continuously across the forest. Nearby locations share information
through spatial correlation, without requiring predefined strata.

Random effects can also enter DBH allocation within species. The
[conditional DBH-effects article](conditional-dbh-effects-plot-sampling.html)
explains that extension with a spatial example and a short stratum alternative.
